events.excerpt: "Train in Python, serve in C++" might as well be Google's motto when it comes to much of its ML work. Python is easy for data scientists to wield, but keeping its interpreter in the serving pipeline can add overhead and deployment headaches. The industry-backed OpenXLA Project provides tools for compiling machine learning computations into native code for different processors. The latest component of this setup to be open sourced is XSE , short for the XLA Serving Engine. One-shot inference XSE is not so much suited for large-scale LLM inference (which would be better served by vLLM or SGLang ), but rather for smaller, more sharply task-oriented models, of which there are plenty at Google. "LLM serving gets most of the attention right now, but a significant amount of production inference is still ranking, recommendation, embedding, and vision models. These tend to be short requests with very high [queries-per-second] and tight latency budgets," Nathan Beach , Google director of product management, wrote in a LinkedIn missive Tuesday. At Google, XSE already handles more than six million queries per second across services including YouTube Shorts, Google Ads, and Search. These models aren't there for a leisurely chat. They rank results, recommend videos, and make other decisions on the fly, often without users noticing. A Python interpreter mulling each request would be a bottleneck, if not the end of Google itself. In Google's tests on short requests, XSE delivered two to five times the throughput of its best optimized Python server, using a quarter of the memory. No Python

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.14061v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems increasingly rely on vector databases containing documents governed by different access-control policies. Recent search-preserving geometric approaches enforce such access control by structuring the embedding space so that transformed embeddings, which we call protected representations, remain retrievable without exposing information across policy boundaries. We provide a unified security analysis of this paradigm, covering policy isolation, representation confidentiality, query forgery resistance, and policy-membership hiding. We consider both a curious cloud service provider observing the protected representations stored in the vector database and a curious user holding aligned pairs of original embeddings and protected representations. Evaluating the available implementations of the works proposing these geometric transformation mechanisms across three encoders, we find that geometric transformations preserve retrieval utility and provide strong policy isolation, but do not provide the other security properties. A curious user can recover the original embeddings from a few hundred pairs and forge policy-compatible queries at a higher cost that grows with encoder dimension for secret per-policy transformations. Moreover, policy-dependent geometry can leak policy membership even when unauthorized retrieval is prevented. These results show that policy isolation, confidentiality, forgery resistance, and membership hiding are distinct security objectives.
events.title: Isolation Is Not Confidentiality: Security Boundaries of Geometric Access Control in RAG

events.excerpt: arXiv:2610.02418v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) are trained on massive, largely unfiltered datasets, including content scraped from nearly every accessible website and user inputs. As a result, LLMs often memorize and reproduce personally sensitive information (PSI) such as birth dates, phone numbers, and home addresses. This leads to significant privacy risks, particularly for high-profile individuals such as executives, politicians, and judges. Existing mitigations largely rely on machine unlearning. However, these methods often remove more information than needed, degrade model utility and safety, and are highly vulnerable to attacks. This paper presents Whiteout, a practical tool that, upon requests by individuals, prevents LLMs from regurgitating their genuine PSIs, by overwriting them using precise and carefully designed obfuscation samples. We evaluate Whiteout on modern LLMs of varying sizes and makers, including a widely-used OpenAI model. Results show that Whiteout effectively prevents disclosure of the targeted PSIs, has negligible impact on model utility and safety, and outperforms existing alternatives. We also test Whiteout against a wide range of countermeasures, from black-box attacks like jailbreaking to white-box adaptive attacks like relearning and quantization. Finally, we conclude with a discussion on the security and ethical implications of Whiteout.
events.title: Mitigating Private Data Leakage in LLMs with Whiteout

events.excerpt: Google DeepMind researchers have completed a formal verification of Signal's messaging security, marking what they claim is the first time AI has helped devise a proof that links protocol-level security guarantees to a widely used cryptographic implementation. They did so using AlphaProof Code, a multi-agent framework for formal software specification and verification. AlphaProof Code relies on a human-guided agent that writes a Lean specification, assesses machine code semantics, and crafts an agent-authored proof that the Lean kernel checks against the specification. In this instance, AlphaProof Code verified Signal’s post-quantum PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet , thereby validating the design of libsignal 's forward secrecy, authentication, post-compromise security, and handshake secrecy. In so doing, the Google/DeepMind team – Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli – has taken a step toward a challenge the Beneficial AI Foundation issued in April to formally verify the Signal protocol and Signal app with Lean. The AlphaProof Code process involves working with various models to turn Signal's security goals into a human-reviewed mathematical specification. Based on this spec, the researchers assigned Gemini Carbon agents to generate Lean code proving the correctness of the libsignal implementation. events.excerpt: Microsoft will enable access to Anthropic's Claude models by default for UK Copilot tenants next month, giving administrators a deadline to decide whether US-based processing fits their compliance requirements. From December 9, UK tenants whose administrators have not already chosen a setting will have Claude access enabled. Administrators can disable it, but leaving the setting untouched means opting in. In this instance, Anthropic operates as a Microsoft subprocessor , and Claude models are already on by default for most customers in the Windows giant's commercial cloud. The exceptions, notably, include the European Union, the European Free Trade Association, and the UK. However, UK tenants aren't in scope for Microsoft's EU Data Boundary - launched at the start of 2023 - and so Redmond is flipping the switch for the country. Anthropic processes the relevant data in the United States, Microsoft's documentation states . Administrators therefore have until December 9 to review whether that meets their organization's data-handling requirements and set access accordingly. Microsoft is also retiring the setting that restricts Claude access to Microsoft 365 alone. "This affirms Microsoft's commitment to offering choice between leading AI models while maintaining enterprise-grade security and compliance," the Redmond-based biz said. So long as you don't mind processing happening in the US. ®
events.title: Microsoft is giving Claude the keys to UK Copilot tenants by default

events.excerpt: v2.11.0 is a hardfork, security and stability release on top of v2.10.3 . It's the public release of v2.11.0-priv , which validators and major RPC providers already run. Uburu hardfork Already active on both networks: Network Fork block Amoy 51978200 Mainnet 96787900 Uburu updates the StateReceiver genesis contract ( 0x…1001 ) at the fork block. It changes how state syncs are executed and recorded. Operators on v2.11.0-priv : same code, switch to v2.11.0 at your next maintenance window. Nodes still on v2.10.3 or older stopped following the chain at the fork block. Upgrade immediately. Highlights Consensus and state sync : state-sync records are fetched from Heimdall one page at a time, as the per-block budget admits them. A failed fetch now fails the block, where before it committed it without state syncs. Span lookups by block number follow Heimdall's rule (the highest-id span containing the block). Locally sealed blocks are checked against whitelisted milestones before they're written. Header verification bounds block numbers and base fees on every import path. Execution : BlockSTM bounds speculative work per block and falls back to serial execution when the bound is hit. Stateless / witnesses : witness messages are bounded on receive, and witness-caused import failures are charged to the peer that served the witness. State serving : snap range serving and state iterators no longer read superseded state layers. Txpool : PIP-15 conditional transactions are off by default. Overdraft checks count queued transactions that will be promoted. RPC and log index : eth_feeHistory n
